metadata.title: How RAG Gives AI Access to External Knowledge
metadata.author: Deepa Shenoy

beats.narration_text: A language model draws on patterns learned during training and on the context it receives. It may not know a specific, current, or private fact you need.

shot.visual_intent: A model node sits between two distinct inputs: learned parameters and supplied context. A small gap marks information that may be current, private, or specific.

beats.narration_text: Imagine asking an assistant: What is our company's remote-work policy? That policy is private, and it may have changed.

shot.visual_intent: A fictional employee asks “What is our company’s remote-work policy?” A locked, labeled company knowledge base appears beside the assistant.

beats.narration_text: That is retrieval-augmented generation: retrieve first, add context, then generate. External sources can include documents, databases, or other approved knowledge sources. The model is not retrained for each question.

shot.visual_intent: Three large animated stages connect in order. A model-weights icon stays unchanged to show no per-question retraining. Show documents and databases as possible sources.

beats.narration_text: This connects to my last video on AI hallucinations: relevant retrieved context can help reduce unsupported claims. But RAG does not guarantee correctness. Retrieval and source quality still matter.

shot.visual_intent: A supported answer is visually tethered to retrieved evidence; then show a broken/weak source warning and “Not a guarantee.” Explicitly connect grounding to the prior hallucinations video.
